title: sCV and F: how variable and forecastable is irradiance
description: Across 68 Spanish weather stations, our forecastability indicator F retains an inverse relationship with forecast error.
text: sCV and F: how variable and how forecastable is solar irradiance How forecastable is the sun? Step 1 of 5 · Compute directly See it on the thread When the link is known, compute it with an explicit model, calibrated and validated on data; learning is added only for a demonstrated benefit. The model at the core. Cyril Voyant · 18 October 2026 Across 68 Spanish weather stations, our forecastability indicator F retains an inverse relationship with forecast error, examined across ten models and 24 horizons. This result, published in Renewable Energy, supports characterising the signal before comparing algorithms: a large error means something different for a regular sky than for a strongly fluctuating irradiance series. The study introduces two complementary indicators. The stochastic coefficient of variation, sCV, measures fluctuations relative to a dynamic clear-sky reference. sCV lies between 0 and 1; the value 1 corresponds to the theoretical case in which the signal switches randomly between clear sky and the diffuse floor. sCV describes signal variability, not a forecast model’s performance against persistence. A value outside the expected domain calls for checking the data, preprocessing and normalisation assumptions. F adds information about temporal dependence through autocorrelation. Two series with similar variability can therefore retain different amounts of memory, leaving different amounts of useful information for prediction. Validation combines one hundred synthetic cyclostationary series with observations from the SIAR network. Simulations allow controlled changes to signal properties; weather stations test the diagnosis against measured conditions. The association between F and forecast errors also appears at individual stations, rather than being solely a consequence of network aggregation. Under extreme synthetic variability, that association can become nonlinear. For an operator or researcher, the contribution is diagnostic: compare forecasting difficulty, select meaningful baselines and interpret a score in context. It can inform a discussion of forecast risk before choosing a more elaborate model. F is neither a calibrated confidence interval nor a promise of financial savings. Overirradiance events and the quality of the clear-sky reference also require attention. The study measures aspects of inherent forecastability; it does not remove atmospheric uncertainty or establish an operational benefit for every energy system. Those benefits require a separate decision-based evaluation. Variability and memory. Teaching illustration from the UE14 course: F changes with the forecast horizon while sCV is held fixed; the bars represent remaining temporal memory. This course illustration is not the paper’s 68-station validation and its values should not be read as a universal threshold. Source: Cyril Voyant, cyrilvoyant.github.io/assets/course/F_horizon.png. Paper, authors and resources Reference: Cyril Voyant, Alan Julien, Milan Despotovic, Gilles Notton, Luis Antonio Garcia-Gutierrez, Claudio Francesco Nicolosi, Philippe Blanc and Jamie Bright. title: sCV et F : variabilité et prévisibilité de l'éclairement
description: Sur 68 stations météorologiques espagnoles, notre indice de prévisibilité F conserve une relation inverse avec l’erreur de prévision.
text: sCV et F : variabilité et prévisibilité de l'éclairement solaire Le ciel change, mais à quel point reste-t-il prévisible ? Étape 1 sur 5 · Calculer directement Le voir sur le fil Quand le lien est connu, on le calcule avec un modèle explicite, calibré et validé sur des données ; on n'ajoute de l'apprentissage que pour un bénéfice démontré. Le modèle au cœur. Cyril Voyant · 18 octobre 2026 Sur 68 stations météorologiques espagnoles, notre indice de prévisibilité F conserve une relation inverse avec l’erreur de prévision, examinée sur dix modèles et 24 horizons. Ce résultat publié dans Renewable Energy montre l’intérêt de caractériser le signal avant de comparer les algorithmes : une erreur élevée ne raconte pas la même histoire sur un ciel régulier et sur une série très fluctuante. Le travail introduit deux indicateurs complémentaires. Le coefficient de variation stochastique, sCV, mesure les fluctuations en les rapportant à une référence dynamique de ciel clair. sCV est compris entre 0 et 1 ; la valeur 1 correspond au cas théorique où le signal alterne aléatoirement entre ciel clair et plancher diffus. sCV décrit la variabilité du signal, pas la performance d’un modèle par rapport à la persistance. Une valeur hors du domaine attendu demande de vérifier les données, le prétraitement et les hypothèses de normalisation. F ajoute une information de dépendance temporelle issue de l’autocorrélation. Deux séries de variabilité comparable peuvent ainsi conserver des mémoires différentes : l’une laisse davantage d’information exploitable pour prévoir. La validation combine cent séries synthétiques cyclostationnaires et les observations du réseau SIAR. Les simulations permettent de faire varier les propriétés du signal ; les stations permettent de confronter le diagnostic à des situations réelles. La relation entre F et les erreurs apparaît aussi à l’échelle des stations, et ne se réduit donc pas à un effet d’agrégation du réseau. Sous forte variabilité synthétique, elle peut devenir non linéaire. Pour un utilisateur, l’apport est un diagnostic : comparer la difficulté de prévision, choisir des références et interpréter un score dans son contexte. F n’est ni un intervalle de confiance calibré ni une promesse de gain économique. Les événements de sur-éclairement et la qualité du modèle de ciel clair demandent aussi de l’attention. L’étude propose une mesure de la prévisibilité ; elle ne supprime pas l’incertitude atmosphérique. Variabilité et mémoire. Illustration pédagogique du cours UE14 : F varie avec l'horizon de prévision quand sCV est fixé ; les barres représentent la mémoire temporelle restante. Cette illustration de cours n'est pas la validation sur 68 stations de l'article, et ses valeurs ne sont pas un seuil universel. title: BLEND: better persistence with no neural network training
description: Accounting for daily phase improves persistence forecasts on the solar series studied, with differences widening at longer lead times.
text: BLEND: a better persistence forecast without training a neural network Better persistence Step 2 of 5 · Hybridize See it on the thread When the model falls short, complete it: keep the model, learn only what is missing. The model at the core. Cyril Voyant · 18 October 2026 Accounting for daily phase improves persistence forecasts on the solar series studied, with differences widening at longer lead times. In our Applied Mathematical Modelling paper, BLEND supplies this baseline directly from raw irradiance, without normalising observations by an external clear-sky model. The starting point is physical and statistical: irradiance does not have the same statistical properties throughout the day. Part of their evolution repeats with the cycle. Simply carrying the latest observation forward misses that structure. BLEND operators combine immediate memory with phase-aligned recurrence. The weight between the two is set for each phase of the cycle. Its MSE-optimal value, written with cyclic means, deviations and correlations, is close to a one-line least-squares fit on past cycles. The simplified coefficient λ = (1 + ρ)/2, also set for each phase from the local correlation ρ, is an approximation under the correlation assumptions of Remark 17, whose performance depends on the horizon. The resulting forecast has an explicit analytical construction rather than a hidden layer fitted to predict the target. Validation combines controlled simulations with measurements from 68 Spanish stations. It compares persistence variants with more elaborate reference methods. On measured data, cyclostationary adjustments reduce errors relative to their naive counterparts; the paper also evaluates inter-model differences with Wilcoxon tests. Error distributions also reveal how performance varies across stations and forecast horizons. The practical contribution is an interpretable, inexpensive analytical baseline against which to assess a trained model. Weights are estimated from historical observations in closed form, without iterative optimisation. Cyclic statistics and correlations therefore require appropriate estimation. BLEND does not outperform every optimised method; autoregressive or learned predictors can do better under some conditions. Public MATLAB code makes the protocol inspectable and supports testing whether this simplicity transfers to another series. That test is more informative than assuming that additional modelling complexity must improve the forecast. The paper’s evidence concerns the studied datasets, rather than a universal ranking of forecasting methods. The horizon changes the comparison. Figure 6 of the public author version: average normalized errors over 68 SIAR stations, from 30 to 360 minutes. Circles and dashed lines show nRMSE; squares and solid lines show nMAE. The BLEND variants are compared with persistence and other references under the study protocol; these averages do not imply that a model wins at every station. Source: arxiv.org/html/2602.18949v3. Full research team and publication below. Open code v1.1.1: an out-of-sample benchmark The corrected MATLAB benchmark separates 6,000 observations for estimation from 6,000 for evaluation, with common forecast targets. It compares 21 references over five horizons and 10 synthetic realisations. The figure below reports day-and-night nRMSE, normalised by the mean of the evaluated observations. BLEND least squares per phase reaches mean nRMSE 0.3020, 0.3975, 0.4447, 0.4880 and 0.4954 at 1, 2, 3, 6 and 9 steps, compared with 0.5021 for cyclic persistence. Its weight is estimated by least squares in closed form, without iterative optimisation. These estimates are not identical to the finite-sample moments estimator in general. CLIPER on the ratio to trend x/CS (clear-sky reference) has the lowest mean errors here. This is consistent with a synthetic signal constructed as clear sky multiplied by correlated noise. CLIPER on the difference from the periodic trend (mean profile estimated on training data) also performs well without a clear-sky reference. Ten realisations of one generator do not establish a universal ranking or reproduce the paper’s SIAR experiments. Archived code v1.1.1 · Full results, figures and CSV · Step-by-step calculation Three panels of out-of-sample nRMSE versus horizon 1 to 9 steps, synthetic signal, 10 realisations (cyclostationary-forecasting-matlab v1.1.1). BLEND on the raw signal: weight per phase 0.302 to 0.495, one weight 0.365 to 0.499, simplified (1 + rho)/2 0.403 to 0.744; cyclic persistence 0.502. CLIPER without clear sky: one weight on the difference from trend 0.223 to 0.354, weight per phase 0.263 to 0.354. With clear sky: CLIPER on x/CS 0.213 to 0.354, BLEND on x/CS 0.219 to 0.413, smart multiplicative 0.230 to 0.593, stochastic 0.260 to 0.474. title: BLEND : meilleure persistance sans réseau neuronal
description: Introduire la phase quotidienne dans une prévision de persistance améliore les résultats sur les séries solaires étudiées.
text: BLEND : une meilleure persistance sans entraîner de réseau neuronal Une meilleure persistance, sans entraîner un réseau neuronal Étape 2 sur 5 · Hybrider Le voir sur le fil Quand le modèle ne suffit pas, on le complète : garder le modèle, n'apprendre que ce qui manque. Le modèle au cœur. Cyril Voyant · 18 octobre 2026 Introduire la phase quotidienne dans une prévision de persistance améliore les résultats sur les séries solaires étudiées, avec des écarts qui s’accentuent aux horizons plus longs. Dans notre travail publié dans Applied Mathematical Modelling, BLEND fournit cette référence directement sur l’éclairement brut, sans normalisation par un modèle externe de ciel clair. Le point de départ est physique et statistique : les propriétés de l’éclairement ne restent pas identiques au cours de la journée. Leur évolution se répète en partie avec le cycle. Une persistance qui reporte simplement la dernière observation ne représente pas cette structure. Les opérateurs BLEND associent mémoire immédiate et récurrence alignée sur la phase ; le poids entre les deux est fixé pour chaque phase du cycle : sa valeur optimale au sens de l’erreur quadratique, écrite avec les moyennes, écarts-types et corrélations cycliques, est proche d’un ajustement par moindres carrés sur les cycles passés. Le coefficient simplifié λ = (1 + ρ)/2, lui aussi fixé pour chaque phase à partir de la corrélation locale ρ, est une approximation sous les hypothèses de corrélation de la remarque 17, dont les performances dépendent de l’horizon. La validation associe simulations contrôlées et mesures de 68 stations espagnoles. Elle compare les variantes de persistance et des références plus élaborées. Sur les observations, les ajustements cyclostationnaires réduisent les erreurs par rapport à leurs homologues naïfs ; le travail évalue aussi les différences entre modèles par des tests de Wilcoxon. Les distributions d’erreur montrent aussi le comportement selon l’horizon et la station. L’intérêt pratique est une référence analytique, lisible et peu coûteuse, à laquelle confronter un modèle appris. Les poids sont estimés sur les observations passées en forme fermée, sans optimisation itérative. Les statistiques cycliques et les corrélations doivent donc être estimées correctement. BLEND ne gagne pas contre toutes les méthodes optimisées ; des modèles autorégressifs ou appris peuvent faire mieux dans certaines conditions. Le code MATLAB public permet de reproduire le protocole et de tester si cette simplicité convient à une autre série, au lieu de supposer que toute complexité supplémentaire sera utile. L'horizon change la comparaison. Figure 6 de la version auteur publique : erreurs normalisées moyennes sur 68 stations SIAR, de 30 à 360 minutes. Cercles et tirets : nRMSE ; carrés et traits pleins : nMAE. Les variantes de BLEND sont comparées à la persistance et à d'autres références selon le protocole de l'étude ; ces moyennes ne signifient pas qu'un modèle gagne à chaque station. Source : arxiv.org/html/2602.18949v3. Équipe complète et publication ci-dessous. Code ouvert v1.1.1 : un benchmark hors échantillon Le benchmark MATLAB corrigé sépare 6 000 observations pour l’estimation et 6 000 pour l’évaluation, avec des cibles de prévision communes. Il compare 21 références, cinq horizons et dix réalisations synthétiques. La figure ci-dessous présente la nRMSE jour et nuit, normalisé par la moyenne des observations évaluées. BLEND par moindres carrés par phase atteint un nRMSE moyen de 0,3020, 0,3975, 0,4447, 0,4880 et 0,4954 à 1, 2, 3, 6 et 9 pas, contre 0,5021 pour la persistance cyclique. Son poids est estimé par moindres carrés en forme fermée, sans optimisation itérative. En échantillon fini, cette estimation n’est pas en général identique à l’estimation par moments. CLIPER sur le rapport à la tendance de ciel clair x/CS obtient ici les plus faibles erreurs moyennes, ce qui est cohérent avec un signal synthétique construit comme le produit du ciel clair par un bruit corrélé. Sans ciel clair, CLIPER sur la différence à la tendance périodique (profil moyen estimé sur l’apprentissage) est également performant. Dix réalisations d’un seul générateur ne démontrent pas un classement universel et ne reproduisent pas les expériences SIAR du papier. title: MIMO-ELM: seven Corsican energy signals, one model
description: At a one-hour horizon, our MIMO-ELM model achieves nRMSE values of 0.179 for solar generation and 0.051 for thermal generation.
text: MIMO-ELM: seven energy signals of Corsica forecast by one model Seven signals, one ELM Step 3 of 5 · Learn frugally See it on the thread When the useful relations are not known well enough, evaluate what the data can teach, with only as much complexity as pays. Complexity only if it pays. Cyril Voyant · 18 October 2026 At a one-hour horizon, our MIMO-ELM model achieves nRMSE values of 0.179 for solar generation and 0.051 for thermal generation, with R² above 0.98 for both series. Total-demand forecasts remain reliable up to five hours ahead within the study. Published in Applied Energy, these results come from six years of hourly data for the Corsican electricity system. The model handles seven variables: total demand, solar, wind, hydropower, thermal generation, bioenergy and imports. Its multiple-input multiple-output architecture uses sliding windows and cyclic encodings to represent memory and seasonal variation. The Extreme Learning Machine retains a random hidden layer and fits its output coefficients analytically, avoiding iterative deep-network training. Evaluation goes beyond an isolated score. The study compares the model with persistence, single-output formulations and an LSTM under a realistic tuning budget. It reports improved skill against the reference methods and small but stable gains over SISO formulations. Wind and bioenergy remain more difficult because of their strong variability. These differences are useful findings in their own right: a shared architecture does not make every energy component equally predictable. For an energy system, the contribution is a common, rapidly fitted framework for several components. It supports joint investigation of production and consumption. Multiple outputs alone, however, do not impose an exact physical energy balance; enforcing conservation requires an explicit constraint or reconciliation procedure. The reported nRMSE values are not percentage improvements over a competitor. They describe the Corsican evaluation protocol. Transfer to another region should be assessed using that region’s data, constraints and forecast horizons, rather than inferred from architecture alone. Seven signals, one forecast horizon. Figure 1 of the public author version: measured and predicted demand, thermal, hydro, solar, wind, bioenergy and imports over approximately 100 winter hours in Corsica, at a one-hour horizon (MW). This selected window illustrates the trajectories; the paper’s full evaluation establishes performance. Source: arxiv.org/html/2508.12764v2. Full author team and publication below. title: MIMO-ELM : sept signaux énergétiques corses, un modèle
description: À une heure d’horizon, notre modèle MIMO-ELM atteint une nRMSE de 0,179 pour le solaire et de 0,051 pour le thermique.
text: MIMO-ELM : sept signaux énergétiques de la Corse prévus par un seul modèle Sept sorties, six ans de données : ce que montre MIMO-ELM Étape 3 sur 5 · Apprendre frugalement Le voir sur le fil Quand les relations utiles ne sont pas suffisamment connues, évaluer ce que les données permettent d'apprendre, avec seulement la complexité qui paie. La complexité seulement si elle paie. Cyril Voyant · 18 octobre 2026 À une heure d’horizon, notre modèle MIMO-ELM atteint une nRMSE de 0,179 pour le solaire et de 0,051 pour le thermique, avec R² supérieur à 0,98 pour ces deux séries. La demande totale conserve des prévisions jugées fiables jusqu’à cinq heures dans l’étude. Ces résultats, publiés dans Applied Energy, proviennent de six années de données horaires du système électrique corse. Le modèle traite sept variables : demande totale, solaire, éolien, hydraulique, thermique, bioénergie et importations. Son architecture multi-entrée multi-sortie utilise des fenêtres glissantes et des encodages cycliques pour représenter la mémoire et les variations saisonnières. L’Extreme Learning Machine garde une couche cachée aléatoire et ajuste les sorties par une résolution analytique, ce qui évite un entraînement profond itératif. La comparaison ne s’arrête pas à un score isolé. Le travail confronte le modèle à la persistance, à des formulations mono-sortie et à un LSTM avec un budget de réglage réaliste. Il rapporte des gains de compétence face aux références et des améliorations modestes mais stables par rapport aux formulations SISO. L’éolien et la bioénergie restent plus difficiles à prévoir, en lien avec leur forte variabilité. Pour un système énergétique, la contribution est de représenter plusieurs composantes dans un même cadre, rapidement ajustable. Cela facilite l’étude conjointe de la production et de la consommation. Mais une sortie multiple ne garantit pas, à elle seule, un bilan énergétique exact : une contrainte physique ou une réconciliation doit être spécifiée pour l’imposer. Les valeurs rapportées ne sont pas des gains en pourcentage contre un concurrent. Elles caractérisent ce protocole corse ; une autre zone doit être évaluée avec ses propres contraintes, données et horizons. Sept signaux à un même horizon. Figure 1 de la version auteur publique : demande, thermique, hydraulique, solaire, éolien, bioénergie et importations mesurés et prévus sur environ 100 heures d'hiver en Corse, à une heure d'horizon (MW). Cette fenêtre illustre les trajectoires ; l'évaluation complète de l'article établit les performances. Source : arxiv.org/html/2508.12764v2. Équipe complète et publication ci-dessous. title: The γ-index: validating displaced solar forecasts
description: In the gamma-index paper’s synthetic experiment, more than 80% of pixels remain acceptable despite an approximately two-kilometre spatial displacement.
text: The γ-index: validating displaced solar forecasts beyond pointwise errors Beyond pointwise errors Step 5 of 5 · Demonstrate trust See it on the thread Judge against a reference, publish code, data and limits, make research findable and reusable. Trust is demonstrated. Cyril Voyant · 18 October 2026 In the gamma-index paper’s synthetic experiment, more than 80% of pixels remain acceptable despite an approximately two-kilometre spatial displacement, a ten-minute time shift and added noise. Pixelwise RMSE nevertheless suggests substantial error. This illustrates the double-penalty problem: a displaced cloud structure is penalised at both its predicted and observed positions. Published in International Journal of Forecasting, Cyril Voyant’s paper transfers an idea from radiotherapy dose verification to the verification of forecast fields. Three tolerances are specified explicitly: spatial distance DTA, time displacement TTA and intensity difference IDT. The method searches for agreement in a neighbourhood, rather than comparing only identical coordinates at an identical instant. The gamma criterion combines normalised discrepancies; a pixel passes when gamma is less than or equal to one. The Gamma Pass Rate, GPR, reports the corresponding proportion, while mean and maximum gamma complete the diagnosis. In the illustration above, tolerances are two kilometres, thirty minutes and 50 W/m². Those values give the result a precise interpretation; they are not a universal verification standard. The experiment does not mean that every two-kilometre displacement is acceptable under every operational requirement. The paper also applies the framework to satellite-derived solar-irradiance fields over Corsica: with the same tolerances, GPR there is about 67–69%, a different experiment from the more than 80% of the synthetic example. Its practical value is distinguishing a small positioning error from a more important physical disagreement. Public MATLAB code supplies the calculation function and a synthetic example; that example does not redistribute restricted satellite observations. Selecting tolerances before model comparison and reporting RMSE alongside gamma keeps the evaluation transparent. Relaxing the tolerances can raise the pass rate without improving the forecast itself. Gamma therefore adds an acceptance question to error measurement rather than replacing every existing score. A separate synthetic illustration. Figure 2 from the public author-manuscript version in temporal-gamma-index (GitHub): observation, prediction, γ map and RMSE map. This version uses the tolerances printed on the plot (1 km, 50 min, 10 W/m²); these differ from the numerical example discussed above. Source: github.com/cyrilvoyant/temporal-gamma-index — Gamma_Index_Cyril_Voyant.pdf. Cyril Voyant. Paper, authors and resources Reference: Cyril Voyant, sole author. A tolerance-based framework for spatiotemporal forecast validation using the γ-index . International Journal of Forecasting 42(4), 1207–1214 (2026). title: Indice γ : valider des prévisions solaires décalées
description: Dans l’expérience synthétique du travail gamma-index, plus de 80 % des pixels restent acceptables malgré un déplacement spatial d’environ deux kilomètres.
text: L'indice γ : valider des prévisions solaires décalées au-delà des erreurs ponctuelles Une prévision décalée peut rester exploitable : le test gamma Étape 5 sur 5 · Démontrer la confiance Le voir sur le fil Juger contre une référence, publier code, données et limites, rendre la recherche trouvable et réutilisable. La confiance se démontre. Cyril Voyant · 18 octobre 2026 Dans l’expérience synthétique du travail gamma-index, plus de 80 % des pixels restent acceptables malgré un déplacement spatial d’environ deux kilomètres, un décalage de dix minutes et un bruit ajouté. La RMSE pixel à pixel donne pourtant une impression de forte erreur. Ce résultat illustre le problème de double pénalité : une structure nuageuse déplacée est pénalisée à son emplacement prévu et à son emplacement observé. Publié dans International Journal of Forecasting, l’article de Cyril Voyant transpose à la prévision de champs une idée issue de la vérification des doses en radiothérapie. Trois tolérances sont fixées explicitement : distance spatiale DTA, décalage temporel TTA et différence d’intensité IDT. La méthode recherche l’accord dans un voisinage plutôt qu’au seul pixel de mêmes coordonnées et au même instant. Le critère gamma combine les écarts normalisés ; un pixel satisfait le test lorsque gamma est inférieur ou égal à un. Le taux de passage, GPR, indique la proportion correspondante ; moyenne et maximum gamma complètent le diagnostic. Dans l’illustration citée, les tolérances sont deux kilomètres, trente minutes et 50 W/m². Elles donnent un sens précis au résultat ; elles ne constituent pas une norme universelle. Le travail applique aussi le cadre à des cartes satellitaires d’éclairement solaire en Corse : avec les mêmes tolérances, le GPR y est d’environ 67–69 %, une autre expérience que les plus de 80 % de l’exemple synthétique. L’intérêt pour un utilisateur est de distinguer un petit défaut de positionnement d’une divergence physique plus importante. Le code MATLAB public fournit la fonction de calcul et un exemple synthétique ; cet exemple ne redistribue pas les observations satellitaires à accès restreint. Choisir les tolérances avant la comparaison et publier la RMSE en complément conserve une lecture transparente. title: NICE metrics: when RMSE hides a forecast difference
description: At a thirty-minute horizon, the NICE study reports a rounded median nRMSE of 0.19 for both an ELM and an autoregressive model.
text: NICE metrics: when RMSE hides a difference between solar forecasts When RMSE hides a difference Step 5 of 5 · Demonstrate trust See it on the thread Judge against a reference, publish code, data and limits, make research findable and reusable. Trust is demonstrated. Cyril Voyant · 18 October 2026 At a thirty-minute horizon, the NICE study reports a rounded median nRMSE of 0.19 for both an ELM and an autoregressive model. The composite NICEΣ score nevertheless gives 0.75 versus 0.77, with a statistically significant difference in the reported test. The finding is more than a change of notation: the evaluation metric changes how effectively forecasts can be distinguished. Published in Sustainable Energy Technologies and Assessments, the study introduces a family based on error norms of orders one, two and three. NICE¹ tracks average errors, NICE² gives more weight to large deviations and NICE³ amplifies extremes. NICEΣ combines those dimensions. A persistence reference places error in the context of the series, rather than normalising solely by mean irradiance. The components therefore describe different aspects of performance instead of assuming that a single conventional error statistic answers every evaluation question. Validation combines Monte Carlo simulations with observations from 68 SIAR stations in Spain. Comparisons include autoregressive models, Extreme Learning and smart persistence. The paper distinguishes a theoretical construction, which depends on strict statistical assumptions, from empirical evaluation. It does not justify substituting a theoretical expression for observed-error calculations without checking those assumptions. In the thirty-minute example, the tests give p < 0.001 for NICEΣ and p = 0.0591 for nRMSE. These values concern that protocol and those distributions; they do not directly measure the economic importance of the improvement. Users can select sensitivity to extreme errors that fits their application while retaining absolute errors and calculation assumptions. The public PV_ELM_pred code documents the components and their average. Relative scores above one should remain visible: persistence can outperform the model being evaluated. What a single score hides. Figure 5 of the public author version: distributions of NICE components and conventional metrics for four models (EL, AR, SP and ARTU) on SIAR data, at a 30-minute horizon. The printed p-values concern the four-model comparison; they are not the pairwise EL–AR tests discussed above. A displayed p = 0.0000 is rounded, not an exactly zero probability. Source: arxiv.org/html/2508.01457v1. Full research team and DOI below. Paper, authors and resources Reference: Cyril Voyant, Milan Despotovic, Luis Garcia-Gutierrez, Rodrigo Amaro e Silva, Philippe Lauret, Ted Soubdhan and Nadjem Bailek. title: Métriques NICE : quand la RMSE ne suffit pas | Cyril Voyant
description: À trente minutes, le tableau de notre étude NICE rapporte une nRMSE médiane arrondie de 0,19 pour un modèle ELM comme pour un modèle autorégressif.
text: Métriques NICE : quand la RMSE masque une différence entre prévisions solaires Même nRMSE, modèles différents : ce que révèle NICE Étape 5 sur 5 · Démontrer la confiance Le voir sur le fil Juger contre une référence, publier code, données et limites, rendre la recherche trouvable et réutilisable. La confiance se démontre. Cyril Voyant · 18 octobre 2026 À trente minutes, le tableau de notre étude NICE rapporte une nRMSE médiane arrondie de 0,19 pour un modèle ELM comme pour un modèle autorégressif. Le score composite NICEΣ donne pourtant 0,75 contre 0,77, avec une différence statistiquement significative dans le test rapporté. Le résultat n’est pas qu’une nouvelle notation : le choix de la métrique change la capacité à distinguer les prévisions. Publié dans Sustainable Energy Technologies and Assessments, le travail propose une famille fondée sur les normes d’erreur d’ordres un, deux et trois. NICE¹ suit les erreurs moyennes, NICE² donne davantage de poids aux grands écarts et NICE³ accentue les valeurs extrêmes. NICEΣ combine ces dimensions. La référence de persistance replace l’erreur dans le contexte de la série, plutôt que de normaliser uniquement par une moyenne d’éclairement. La validation associe simulations Monte-Carlo et observations de 68 stations SIAR en Espagne. Elle compare notamment modèles autorégressifs, Extreme Learning et persistance intelligente. L’article distingue une construction théorique, dépendante d’hypothèses statistiques strictes, de l’évaluation empirique ; il ne recommande pas de substituer aveuglément une formule théorique au calcul sur observations. Dans l’exemple à trente minutes, les tests donnent p < 0,001 pour NICEΣ et p = 0,0591 pour nRMSE. Ces nombres concernent ce protocole et ces distributions : ils ne mesurent pas directement l’importance économique du gain. L’utilisateur peut choisir une sensibilité aux erreurs extrêmes adaptée à son besoin, tout en conservant les erreurs absolues et les hypothèses de calcul. Le code public PV_ELM_pred documente les composantes et leur moyenne. Un score relatif supérieur à un doit rester visible : la référence de persistance peut être battue, mais aussi faire mieux que le modèle testé. Ce qu'un score unique masque. Figure 5 de la version auteur publique : distributions des composantes NICE et des métriques classiques pour quatre modèles (EL, AR, SP et ARTU) sur les données SIAR, à 30 minutes. Les valeurs p imprimées concernent la comparaison des quatre modèles, pas les tests EL–AR par paires discutés plus haut. Un p = 0,0000 affiché est arrondi, pas une probabilité exactement nulle. It combines simplified representations of lighting, ventilation, auxiliary loads, traffic patterns, seasonal effects and stochastic events such as p… Read the full post Haytham El-Houari and Cyril Voyant The Tunnel Load Simulator is an open-source Streamlit application developed within the SmartTunnel project to generate synthetic electrical load profiles for road tunnels. It combines simplified representations of lighting, ventilation, auxiliary loads, traffic patterns, seasonal effects and stochastic events such as pollution episodes or accidents. The tool produces high-resolution time series, typically at a 10-minute time step, and uses Monte Carlo simulations to represent uncertainty and operational variability. The main strength of the simulator is its transparency: the assumptions, equations and code are openly available. It is also reproducible and citable, with a GitHub repository, MIT license, citation metadata and Zenodo DOI. The model separates the main physical and operational components of tunnel electricity demand, making the results easier to interpret than a purely black-box approach. Scientific and practical interest This tool is not intended to replace measured tunnel data or a calibrated engineering model. Its value is to provide a first-order synthetic generator for prototyping, sensitivity analysis, teaching and preliminary energy-system studies. It can help explore how tunnel length, traffic, lighting, ventilation, slope, altitude and random events affect electricity demand. It also provides a useful basis for future work on calibration, forecasting, photovoltaic coupling and storage sizing. Key message The Tunnel Load Simulator is a transparent, open-source and citable research-software demonstrator for synthetic road-tunnel electricity demand. Its current role is to support early-stage modelling and discussion; with calibration on real tunnel data, it could become a stronger tool for tunnel energy analysis and management. Younis , Maher Jebali & Rabab Triki Diffuse solar radiation remains one of the most complex components of the solar resource, particularly in regions affected by aerosols, humidity, and strong climatic contrasts. Read the full post Measurement and forecasting of the diffuse fraction of solar irradiance using a hybrid stacking model in Saudi Arabia Diffuse solar radiation remains one of the most complex components of the solar resource, particularly in regions affected by aerosols, humidity, and strong climatic contrasts. In this study, diffuse irradiance measurements collected across six representative stations in Saudi Arabia were combined with a hybrid stacking framework integrating Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and LightGBM to analyze and forecast the diffuse fraction of solar irradiance. The work simultaneously explores the physical variability of diffuse radiation and its short-term predictability under desert, coastal, and high-altitude atmospheric conditions. Results, impact and perspectives Paper accepted in Scientific Reports: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-49910-4 Scientific impact: The analysis revealed strong spatial variability in diffuse solar regimes across Saudi Arabia. Coastal stations such as Jeddah reached diffuse fraction values close to 0.95, reflecting intense aerosol and humidity-driven scattering, while inland desert stations remained dominated by direct beam irradiance. The proposed stacking model significantly improved predictive skill compared with standalone learners, with forecast correlations between 0.94 and 0.97, and error reductions reaching 62.48% in some seasonal configurations. These results confirm that diffuse fraction dynamics are strongly climate-dependent and can be effectively learned through hybrid ensemble modeling. Operational impact: Accurate prediction of diffuse fraction directly affects photovoltaic yield estimation, tilted irradiance transposition, bifacial PV modeling, and solar resource assessment in regions exposed to strong aerosol or humidity variability. The framework offers a practical tool for improving solar forecasting in operational environments where atmospheric conditions evolve rapidly. Key message: Understanding how the atmosphere redistributes sunlight is not only a physical challenge; it is also a forecasting problem with direct implications for next generation photovoltaic systems . BLEND combines the latest observation with an observation aligned to the target phase of the cycle. The weights are estimated from historical observations in closed form. Phase-wise least squares provides an explicit baseline without iterative optimisation; a moments-based formulation is equivalent in population under its assumptions, but need not give exactly the same finite-sample estimate. The paper evaluates these operators on controlled simulations and 68 SIAR stations. The separate open-code benchmark v1.1.1 uses held-out synthetic data and compares 21 references, including variants with and without a clear-sky model. It illustrates when phase information helps, without establishing a universal ranking. Scientific contribution: a phase-aware analytical reference for comparing solar forecasts. The original raw-signal BLEND formulation does not require an external clear-sky model; the extended code also includes clear-sky-based variants, explicitly identified in the benchmark. Practical use: inspect the assumptions, estimate parameters on past data, and evaluate on unseen observations. The synthetic code results and the measured-data results of the paper are separate experiments. Published online 28 March 2026 · Energy: forecasting and systems From Pixels to Tolerances: Rethinking Forecast Validation with the γ-Index Cyril Voyant Classical metrics like RMSE evaluate forecasts as if every pixel must match perfectly in space and time. Machines optimize for that. Humans do not think that way. Read the full post Cyril Voyant Classical metrics like RMSE evaluate forecasts as if every pixel must match perfectly in space and time. Machines optimize for that. Humans do not think that way. This work introduces a tolerance-based framework using the γ-index, where forecasts are evaluated within physically meaningful margins (space, time, intensity). The originality lies in shifting from exact matching to acceptable agreement. It bridges human operational reasoning and machine evaluation: a forecast slightly shifted but physically coherent is no longer “wrong” : it is usable Results, impact and perspectives The study demonstrates that classical pixel-wise metrics suffer from a structural limitation known as the double penalty: a small spatial or temporal shift leads to both a miss and a false alarm, artificially inflating the error. In controlled experiments, such shifts can produce large RMSE values (e.g., ~20–40 W/m²), even when the underlying physical structure is preserved. The γ-index resolves this by embedding tolerances directly into the evaluation. Instead of penalizing displacement, it checks whether the forecast lies within an acceptable region in a joint space–time–intensity domain. The results are clear: Mean γ remains stable (~0.29–0.35), showing robustness to small displacements γ Passing Rate (GPR) reaches ~67–69% on the HelioClim-3 satellite maps, capturing operational usability (the “more than 80%” quoted elsewhere comes from the separate synthetic experiment) RMSE, in contrast, reacts strongly to minor misalignments and can misclassify usable forecasts as failures This changes the interpretation of performance. The question is no longer “Is the forecast exact?” but “Is it operationally acceptable?” For the community, this has direct implications: Energy systems: avoids unnecessary corrective actions (e.g., battery dispatch, backup generation) Meteorology: provides a unified and physically interpretable validation criterion AI/ML: opens the door to tolerance-aware learning, where γ can be embedded as a constraint or loss term The next step is important: moving from validation to learning. The γ-index is continuous and almost everywhere differentiable, making it compatible with optimization frameworks. This suggests a new paradigm where models are not trained to minimize pixel errors, but to respect physical tolerances. In short, the γ-index is more than a metric. Dans ce contexte, la question n’est plus seulement de produire du savoir, mais d’en garantir la visibilité, la robustesse et la réutilisabilité. Read the full post Cyril Voyant La production scientifique mondiale connaît une croissance sans précédent, amplifiée par l’essor des modèles d’intelligence artificielle générative. Dans ce contexte, la question n’est plus seulement de produire du savoir, mais d’en garantir la visibilité, la robustesse et la réutilisabilité. Cette page présente un cadre structurant de l’excellence scientifique fondé sur une approche systémique et multiplicative. La dynamique actuelle se caractérise par une augmentation rapide du volume de publications une hybridation croissante entre production humaine et assistée par IA une dilution du signal scientifique dans un bruit informationnel massif Un résultat rigoureux mais non accessible devient structurellement invisible. Une approche systémique de l’excellence L’excellence scientifique ne doit plus être considérée comme une propriété intrinsèque, mais comme un système reposant sur plusieurs dimensions interdépendantes. Fondations Rigueur (R) Transparence (T) Visibilité (V) Adoptabilité (A) Amplificateurs Collaboration (C) Ouverture (O) Signification sociétale (S) Formulation du cadre RTVACOS E∝(R×T×V×A)×(1+C+O+S) Cette formulation repose sur deux principes : multiplicativité des fondations → si une dimension est nulle, l’impact global s’annule effet amplificateur non compensatoire → les dimensions secondaires amplifient uniquement un socle solide Du SEO au GEO : un changement de paradigme La visibilité scientifique ne repose plus uniquement sur les citations humaines. Elle dépend désormais de la capacité des systèmes à : identifier des entités (auteurs, méthodes, données) exploiter des métadonnées structurées relier contenus, code et jeux de données Éléments clés : identifiants persistants (ORCID, DOI) métadonnées explicites dépôts ouverts (code, données) knowledge graphs redondance contrôlée entre plateformes Un contenu non structuré devient invisible pour les systèmes génératifs. RTVACOS : un cadre réflexif, non normatif qui n’a pas vocation à produire un score. Il permet : d’identifier les faiblesses structurelles d’un travail, d’éviter les effets de compensation artificielle, de guider les bonnes pratiques scientifiques. Toute instrumentalisation (optimisation superficielle, métriques vides) en annule la portée. Implications opérationnelles et pour les chercheurs : maintenir une identité numérique cohérente publier code et données structurer les métadonnées documenter les processus (y compris échecs) Pour les institutions : dépasser les indicateurs volumétriques valoriser reproductibilité et réutilisabilité investir dans les compétences data/metadata Conclusion : La rigueur reste nécessaire mais insuffisante. L’excellence scientifique devient une question d’ingénierie de la connaissance : structurer, relier et diffuser les savoirs pour assurer leur existence effective dans un écosystème algorithmique. Read the full post Fast, transparent, and operational short-term forecasting of demand and generation across multiple energy sources. Modern power systems are becoming structurally more complex. Renewable integration, self-consumption, distributed resources, and partial interconnections introduce strong variability and cross-dependencies between energy sources. In this context, forecasting is no longer about predicting a single time series. It is about predicting a system. A new study published in Applied Energy presents a unified Multi-Input Multi-Output Extreme Learning Machine (MIMO-ELM) framework designed for short-term forecasting of multi-source energy systems. The model simultaneously predicts seven grid variables: total demand and generation from solar PV, wind, hydropower, thermal power, bioenergy, and imports. What the study shows Using six years of hourly data from Corsica, the MIMO-ELM framework jointly forecasts seven variables: total demand and generation from solar PV, wind, hydropower, thermal power, bioenergy and imports. At a one-hour horizon, the published study reports nRMSE values of 0.179 for solar generation and 0.051 for thermal generation , with R² above 0.98 for both series. Total-demand forecasts remain reliable up to five hours ahead within this study. Comparisons with persistence and LSTM must be read with the reported data split, tuning budget and computational constraints. The multi-output formulation represents several responses in one model. It does not, by itself, impose an exact energy balance. Physical conservation requires an explicit constraint or reconciliation step. Published article: Applied Energy 410, 127599 (2026) · Read the full research story in English and French . 2026 · Research practice Invisible Research Has No Impact: Engineering Scientific Influence in the AI Era Cyril Voyant The research landscape has shifted from scarcity to saturation: producing knowledge is no longer the bottleneck: being discovered, trusted, and reused is. Read the full post Cyril Voyant The research landscape has shifted from scarcity to saturation: producing knowledge is no longer the bottleneck: being discovered, trusted, and reused is. In an AI-accelerated environment, impact follows attention dynamics and depends on visibility, transparency, and operational adoption rather than venue prestige alone. Work that cannot be found or verified remains effectively nonexistent. Discoverability, metadata quality, reproducibility, and clear failure modes have become integral parts of the scientific method. Rigor builds credibility, transparency builds trust, and usability enables adoption. Visibility is not vanity; it is the infrastructure that allows knowledge to circulate and survive algorithmic filtering. Outreach and collaboration amplify impact only when foundations are solid. In this context, publishing is necessary but insufficient: impact must be engineered. Research that remains invisible delays innovation and contributes little to practice. The objective is no longer to publish more, but to ensure that robust knowledge is discoverable, credible, and usable. The methodology combines synthetic Monte Carlo simulations with real-world data from the Spanish SIAR network, encompassing 68 meteorological stations in diverse climatic regions. Forecasting models evaluated include autoregressive approaches, Extreme Learning Machines, and smart persistence. Results show that theoretical and empirical NICEᵏ values converge only when strong statistical assumptions are met (e.g., R² ≈ 1.0 for NICE²). Most importantly, the composite metric NICEΣ consistently outperforms conventional metrics in discriminating between models (e.g., p-values < 0.05 for NICEΣ vs > 0.05 for nRMSE or nMAE). Across increasing forecast horizons, NICEΣ yields consistently significant p-values (from 10⁻⁶ to 0.004), while nRMSE and nMAE often fail to reach statistical significance. Furthermore, traditional metrics (nRMSE, nMAE, nMBE, R²) cannot reliably distinguish between models in head-to-head comparisons. In contrast, the NICEᵏ family demonstrates superior statistical discrimination (p < 0.001), broader variance distributions, and better inter-study comparability. This study confirms the theoretical and empirical validity of the NICEᵏ framework and highlights its operational relevance. It establishes NICEᵏ as a robust, unified, and interpretable alternative to conventional metrics for evaluating deterministic solar forecasting models. Deterministic and probabilistic results are compared to traditional benchmarks, including ARMA with McClear-generated Clearsky data and quantile regression for probabilistic forecasts. ELM matches or outperforms these methods, providing accurate predictions and robust uncertainty quantification. This approach offers a simple, efficient solution for real-time solar forecasting. Twenty Years of Publishing: Why Open Access Is No Longer Optional Twenty Years of Forecasting: Why Parsimony Beats Complexity I've experienced this troubling phenomenon firsthand: an article I had little hope for exploded with hundreds of citations, while another piece I considered my best work remained in obscurity. After twenty years of research, one thing is clear: in a rapidly evolving academic ecosystem, publishing alone is no longer sufficient. A Saturated Ecosystem The explosion has been brutal. In the international journals I work with, submissions have surged by over 30% in recent years. Rejection rates now reach 70% in some disciplines. Even more striking: the geography of research has been radically transformed. Where the United States dominated fifteen years ago, China now represents over 40% of global submissions in many fields. This quantitative explosion masks deeper transformations. The emergence of AI-assisted writing tools facilitates large-scale manuscript production. Some countries have implemented financial incentives that can reach $43,000 for a publication in Nature or Science - peaks observed in China between 2008 and 2016. The result? Between 10% and 30% of scientific articles remain uncited several years after publication, depending on the discipline. This isn't always a quality issue: it's often a discoverability problem. In this saturated environment, visibility has become a scientific skill in its own right. Before Submission: Preparing for Discoverability Visibility work begins well before submission. A title of 8-15 words, precise without jargon, an explicit abstract, and keywords covering the terminological variants of your field significantly improve findability via Google Scholar. Search engines first index the metadata you provide them. Journal selection deserves strategic reflection that's often overlooked. The question isn't "which journal is most prestigious?" but "where does my audience actually read?" Publishing in a highly ranked journal but in a field distant from yours may flatter the ego, but sometimes has less impact than a second-tier journal that's central to your niche. Metrics like CiteScore (measuring average citations over 4 years) or the "Cites per document" indicator on SCImago help choose a journal actually read by your peers. Better to publish "in the conversation" than "beside the conversation." Open Access: A Global Opportunity The open access movement has created unprecedented opportunities for research visibility. Repository platforms like arXiv (multidisciplinary), medRxiv (health), or EarthArXiv (Earth sciences) accelerate the circulation of ideas. In many fields, a preprint signals scientific openness, generates early feedback, and can initiate citations before formal publication. For researchers in Europe, national agreements often allow avoiding open access publication fees. Simply linking your institutional email and ORCID identifier can automatically provide these benefits. This "green" strategy ensures worldwide free availability of your work. Concretely: even if your article is published in a journal with a $3,000 annual subscription, anyone in the world can freely access your repository version after the embargo period. Writing to Be Discovered A principle I now apply: one idea equals one article, adaptable according to disciplines. Multi-subject manuscripts get lost in the crowd. I prefer short formats for targeted results - they're often more read and cited than very dense articles. It's about doing "academic SEO": aligning title, abstract, keywords, and subheadings with your audience's typical queries. Make your figures self-sufficient with explanatory captions and clear licenses (like Creative Commons) to encourage reuse. Systematically deposit your datasets and scripts following FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable). A Data Management Plan from the beginning of a project facilitates this approach. A GitHub repository with DOI via Zenodo increases reuse and mentions, making you discoverable by completely different audiences. For licenses, favor Creative Commons (CC-BY for example) which allows reuse with attribution. Open access isn't limited to "Green" (repository deposit) or "Gold" (direct paid publication): the emerging "Diamond" model offers free access for everyone. After Publication: Orchestrating Dissemination Publication day isn't the end of the story, it's the beginning of your research's public life. I now apply a reproducible plan: Immediate: Deposit the accepted version in institutional repository with ORCID synchronization. This step takes 10 minutes and ensures permanent archiving. Professional: Targeted announcement on LinkedIn in 3-4 sentences explaining the question your article answers, a key result, and why it matters. This is where you'll reach decision-makers and industry leaders who can transform your results into action. General public: A short popularization post on Medium or a blog explaining the "why" and potential uses. Some research deserves to influence public debate. Academic: Sharing on ResearchGate and Academia.edu while respecting publisher policies. Necessary vigilance: Only massively disseminate quality work - otherwise we contribute to the information noise we denounce. Structural Solutions Needed Beyond individual strategies, reforms are necessary. Researchers excel in fundamental research (Nobel prizes and Fields medals attest to this). But they are increasingly absent from editorial boards of major applied journals, particularly in strategic fields. Structural solutions could include: Revising valorization policies by placing quality at the center, with minimum thresholds over 2 years rather than a quantity race Recruiting dedicated administrative staff to free researchers from management tasks Recognizing editorial functions in career evaluation Training in "publication literacy" from the PhD level In a saturated landscape where we must navigate between global quantitative explosion and quality maintenance, visibility becomes an impact multiplier. An article in a top journal is good. An article that people find, read, use, and build upon for their own research is infinitely better. Visibility isn't academic vanity: it's the necessary condition for years of research to find their social, economic, and scientific utility.
